title: SIU launches probe after cop kills man; 37-year-old Amherstburg resident shot
article: Lisa Stewart wailed helplessly as her common-law husband lay mortally wounded outside their Amherstburg home.
Robert Scott Carpenter, 37, was shot Monday by an Amherstburg police officer during a confrontation which left one of the officer's colleagues with knife wounds to his face.
"She was crying and saying 'I love you, I love you,' and he was talking back," a neighbour said, describing Stewart's reaction.
"She was very upset. I was hanging on to her and she almost fell over."

Mr. Carpenter was shot shortly after 7 a.m. when Amherstburg police responded to a domestic situation after a disrupted 911 call by Stewart, said a police source late Monday night. Efforts to revive him failed and he was pronounced dead three hours later at Hotel-Dieu Grace Hospital.
An autopsy was scheduled for today.
The source said when police arrived Stewart was outside screaming that her common-law husband had the children inside. Mr. Carpenter was shot once after he lunged at an officer with a knife.
While the province's Special Investigations Unit wouldn't provide any details, Janet Carpenter said her only son was shot in "the femoral artery in his groin and bled to death."
In a twist of fate, Mr. Carpenter's eldest sister, who works in the nuclear medicine department at Hotel-Dieu Grace, was on duty when her brother died in hospital.
Amherstburg Police Chief Brian Bird would not comment on the incident, referring all questions to the SIU.
Other than saying one police officer suffered "non-life- threatening" injuries during the incident and confirming Mr. Carpenter was killed by a police officer, the SIU released little information.

A witness to events immediately prior to the shooting said an Amherstburg officer arrived in his cruiser at Mr. Carpenter's 258 McCurdy Dr. home about 7:10 or 7:15 a.m. There were no sirens and no sense of urgency. The witness heard yelling and screaming and a struggle as the officer approached the front door.
Someone inside tried to prevent the officer from entering and, as the two wrestled with the door, Stewart came "rolling out, head over heels on to the front lawn."

The woman said Mr. Carpenter had been acting erratically and that objects in the front yard had been smashed overnight. She also said Mr. Carpenter seemed paranoid lately and that her husband helped him install motion detectors at his house Sunday.

At some point, the woman said, a second police officer arrived at the house. After the shooting -- which she didn't see or hear -- the woman saw that the second officer, who she identified as Sgt. Bart DiPasquale, a veteran of the department, was injured.
"He was bent over and vomiting and he had a cut on his forehead," she said.
Both officers were taken to the emergency department at Windsor Regional Hospital's Western campus, where they were treated and released for non-life- threatening injuries.
DiPasquale, who the source confirmed was not the shooter, reportedly suffered bruising and abrasions over his left eye.
The younger police officer at the scene also suffered bruising to his face and neck.
Medical officials said both officers were "shell-shocked" by the shooting.
The quiet, tree-lined street where the incident occurred is likely to remain blocked off for several days, said Jon Ansell of the province's SIU.
The SIU was notified by Amherstburg police of the shooting about 8:30 a.m. and a team of six investigators -- including two forensic identification specialists -- was sent to the scene.
The SIU is a civilian agency that investigates all incidents involving civilians and police resulting in serious injury, sexual assault or death.
Prior to their arrival, the OPP secured the scene around Mr. Carpenter's home, where he had lived for more than three years with Stewart, his companion of five years and mother of his two children.
Officers with LaSalle, Essex and Amherstburg police set up a secondary police line more than 200 metres away in both directions.

Reporters were not allowed any closer and residents of the middle- class neighbourhood of single-family homes -- many pushing strollers or toting toddlers by the hand -- were escorted to their doors by police.

Two of Mr. Carpenter's sisters -- he has three: Sherry, Shelly and Stacy -- arrived about 11 a.m. to pick up the couple's children. Sarah, 3 and Noah, 2, were led by the hand under the police tape and whisked away in a van.

The toddlers were home at the time of the incident and Sarah may have witnessed the shooting, said a neighbour who took care of the children when Stewart rushed to the hospital to be at Mr. Carpenter's bedside.
"The little girl knows what happened. I think she saw it. She's talking about it. She said 'Daddy had blood and he's gone to the hospital,'" said the neighbour, who asked not to be identified.

"His life revolved around those kids. He was devoted to them. He worshipped them," said Mr. Carpenter's mother. "He always got along with everyone. He could walk into a room and make 20 friends in five minutes."
Mr. Carpenter was born and raised in Windsor and is a graduate of Centennial High School. He has another child, Kyle, 12, who lives with his mother in Barrie.

Mr. Carpenter's mother said he was a talented guitarist who often sang to his young children. He used to play gigs at the CanUsa, a bar in Windsor, with his band Night Breed and formerly taught music at Leone's Music World.

Carpenter once worked at Trident Compressed Air and was an assembler at DaimlerChrylser's Pillette Road van plant until he suffered a back and groin injury about three years ago and was on disability, said his mother.
